# Cache-Aside: Hit Rate and Staleness

Banks and exchanges put a **key-value cache** (Redis, Memcached, Aerospike) in front of nearly every slow store: instrument reference data, client limits, the latest prices. The usual pattern is **cache-aside**: look in the cache; if the key isn't there (a *miss*), read the database and put the answer in the cache for next time.

Caching makes reads fast. The hard part is everything else: the cache holds only some of the keys, so something must be **evicted**; and the database keeps changing, so a cached copy can go **stale**. The question: **what really decides the hit rate, and how do you stop serving out-of-date data?**

How the cells run:

- **The simulation is an HTML cell** that runs 100,000 requests in a few tens of milliseconds, live from the controls: move one and it runs again. It's a model, not a real Redis, but with the same rules.
- **JavaScript** measures every eviction policy at every cache size.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**, then play with the controls.

## 1. The cache

> Controls, 900 pixels wide: a slider "Cache size (entries, of 10,000 keys)" bound to kv_size, 10 to 5,000 in steps of 10, default 500; a dropdown "Eviction policy" bound to kv_policy with LRU, LFU, FIFO and Random (values LRU, LFU, FIFO, random), default LRU; a slider "Time to live (seconds, 0 = never expires)" bound to kv_ttl, 0 to 60, default 0; a slider "Database changes per second" bound to kv_updates, 0 to 200 in steps of 10, default 20; and a dropdown "When the database changes a value" bound to kv_writes with "Leave the cache alone (only the TTL helps)" (ttl) and "Delete the cached copy" (delete), default ttl.

- **Zipf popularity**: the most popular key is asked for twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on. Real access patterns (a few instruments, a few clients) look like this.
- **Eviction policies**: LRU throws out the key used longest ago, LFU the key used least often, FIFO the key added longest ago, Random any key.
- **The defaults start with the problem**: no expiry, and the cache left alone when the database changes.

## 2. Watch it run

> Simulate a cache-aside cache in front of a slow database, live from the controls in nb: 100,000 requests at 2,000 a second for 10,000 keys with Zipf popularity, the database answering in 15 to 40 ms and the cache in under 1 ms, and the database changing nb.kv_updates keys a second (popular keys more often). Implement LRU, LFU (in O(1) with frequency groups), FIFO and random eviction, a time to live, and an option to delete the cached copy when the database changes. Show tiles for the hit rate, the median, 99th-percentile and average request time and the share of reads that returned out-of-date data, a line describing the setup, and a histogram of request times in 1 ms bins on a log scale, cache reads green and database reads amber. Re-run whenever a control moves. Dark theme.

- **Two humps**: requests answered by the cache take well under a millisecond, the rest 15 to 40 ms. The average lands in between, and the 99th percentile sits in the database hump unless the hit rate is very high.
- **The red tile is the one to watch.** With the defaults, over a third of the cache's answers are out of date: the popular keys are also the ones that change most.
- **Then try**: a TTL of 5 seconds; then *Delete the cached copy*. Which one fixes it?

## 3. Every policy, every size

> In JavaScript, with the same model and the cached copy deleted on every change, measure the hit rate of all four policies at cache sizes of 50, 100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000 and 5,000 entries, print a table and the average request time with a 500-entry LRU cache against almost no cache, and return a Vega-Lite line chart of hit rate against cache size (log scale), one line per policy.

The live view shows one setting; this cell measures 28. Copies are deleted on every change here, so no answer is ever stale.

## What the run shows

With a 500-entry LRU cache (5% of the keys) and 20 database changes a second:

| when the database changes | hit rate | out-of-date reads |
|---|---|---|
| leave the cache alone, no TTL | 58.4% | 36.42% |
| leave the cache alone, TTL 5 s | 58.2% | 24.73% |
| delete the cached copy | 57.9% | 0.00% |

- **Caching 5% of the keys answers 58% of the requests**, because popularity is so skewed. The average request drops from 27.5 ms with almost no cache to 12.0 ms. The median is under half a millisecond.
- **But the tail doesn't move.** The 99th percentile is still 39.9 ms: with a 58% hit rate, more than 1 request in 100 goes to the database. To improve p99, the hit rate has to pass 99%.
- **Staleness is the real danger, and a TTL barely helps.** Leaving the cache alone, over a third of cached answers were out of date: the most popular keys are also the most often changed. A 5-second TTL still left a quarter stale. Deleting the cached copy when the database changes cost half a percentage point of hit rate and removed stale reads entirely.
- **LFU beats LRU at every size** under this steady, skewed load: 42.5% against 30.5% at 50 entries, 64.9% against 57.9% at 500, and nearly level (87.2% against 86.7%) at 5,000. FIFO and random trail LRU by about 4 points. LFU's weakness, being slow to forget keys that *used* to be popular, never shows here because popularity never changes.
- **Hit rate grows with the logarithm of the cache size**: each doubling adds about 8 points, until most of the popular keys fit.


## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **Predict, then slide.** Set the database changes to 200 a second with copies deleted on change. Will the hit rate fall a little or a lot? Move the slider.
- **Write-through.** Press ✨ on the HTML cell and add: *"Add a third choice: write the new value into the cache when the database changes, and count the extra cache writes."*
- **A cold start.** Press ✨ on the HTML cell and add: *"Plot the hit rate over time in 1-second steps, starting from an empty cache."* How long does it take to warm up?
- **Stampede.** Press ✨ on the HTML cell and add: *"Give every entry the same 10-second TTL and show how many database reads happen in each second."* That's why real caches add a little randomness to TTLs.
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the HTML cell and ask how the LFU cache evicts in constant time.
